emergency_protocols.description: Cardiac Arrest usually reflects acute myocardial ischemia, electrical instability, or pump failure. Patients commonly present with absent pulse, apnea, cyanosis and may suddenly deteriorate because coronary perfusion or rhythm becomes unstable, putting them at risk of shock, pulmonary edema, or cardiac arrest. Early treatment limits avoidable complications and supports safer definitive care.
immediate_actions: For Cardiac Arrest, place the patient on continuous ECG monitoring and secure IV access.
Obtain a 12-lead ECG, bedside glucose, and cardiac biomarkers while checking blood pressure and oxygen saturation.
Alert Emergency Medicine immediately for reperfusion, cardioversion, antiarrhythmic treatment, or ICU transfer as indicated.
do_not: Do not allow exertion or oral intake.
Do not delay rhythm monitoring.
Do not ignore hypotension or diaphoresis.
stabilization_steps: Maintain continuous cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry for Cardiac Arrest.
Titrate oxygen, anti-ischemic, antiarrhythmic, or vasoactive therapy as indicated.
Repeat ECGs and bedside echocardiography, and transfer to coronary care or ICU if instability persists.
emergency_protocols.follow_up_care: Cardiology follow-up for Cardiac Arrest with rhythm review, medication optimization, risk-factor control, and cardiac rehabilitation or device planning.
emergency_protocols.remarks: For Cardiac Arrest, persistent hypotension, recurrent chest pain, or syncope after treatment are red flags that warrant immediate escalation; do not delay rhythm reassessment or reperfusion planning.

emergency_protocols.description: Ischemic Stroke usually arises from acute brain ischemia, hemorrhage, or uncontrolled neuronal activity. Patients commonly present with facial droop, unilateral weakness, slurred speech and may rapidly worsen because cerebral injury can expand, threaten the airway, or leave permanent neurologic disability if treatment is delayed. immediate_actions: For Ischemic Stroke, check capillary glucose, protect the airway, and perform a focused neurologic examination.
Arrange urgent CT brain or MRI and begin seizure control or blood pressure management as appropriate.
Notify Neurology early and activate stroke, seizure, or neurosurgical pathways without delay.
do_not: Do not give food or drink.
Do not lower blood pressure aggressively unless ordered.
Do not delay imaging for routine paperwork.
stabilization_steps: Maintain airway protection and head-of-bed positioning as appropriate.
Monitor consciousness, pupils, and neurologic deficits at frequent intervals.
Escalate to stroke unit, ICU, or neurosurgical care depending on imaging and response.
emergency_protocols.follow_up_care: Neurology follow-up for Ischemic Stroke with imaging review, rehabilitation, antiepileptic or antithrombotic adjustment, and secondary prevention.
emergency_protocols.remarks: For Ischemic Stroke, new weakness, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, or declining consciousness are emergency warning signs; avoid delaying repeat neurologic examination or imaging.

emergency_protocols.description: Severe Asthma Attack usually results from airflow obstruction, lung collapse, or impaired gas exchange. Patients commonly present with wheeze, speaking in words, accessory muscle use and may progress quickly to hypoxemia, hypercapnia, or respiratory arrest when ventilation is not restored promptly. Early treatment limits avoidable complications and supports safer definitive care.
immediate_actions: For Severe Asthma Attack, give oxygen, sit the patient upright if tolerated, and assess the work of breathing.
Obtain arterial blood gas testing and chest imaging or bedside ultrasound to define the cause.
Start bronchodilator, decompression, or ventilatory support measures and involve Pulmonology early.
do_not: Do not give sedatives unless essential.
Do not let the patient walk if oxygenation is poor.
Do not delay ventilatory support.
stabilization_steps: Maintain oxygenation with noninvasive or invasive ventilation when required.
Treat the reversible chest or airway cause and repeat blood gas assessment.
Escalate to ICU if hypoxemia, hypercapnia, or fatigue persists.
emergency_protocols.follow_up_care: Pulmonology or critical care follow-up for Severe Asthma Attack with spirometry, imaging review, inhaler or ventilatory optimization, and rehabilitation.
emergency_protocols.remarks: For Severe Asthma Attack, silent hypoxia, fatigue, tracheal deviation, or rising carbon dioxide are danger signs; do not rely on a single normal examination if the work of breathing is increasing.

emergency_protocols.description: Road Traffic Trauma usually follows blunt or penetrating injury with possible hidden bleeding, fracture, or organ damage. immediate_actions: For Road Traffic Trauma, immobilize the injury, control bleeding, and perform a trauma primary survey.
Document distal pulses, motor function, and sensation, then obtain urgent imaging or FAST/CT as needed.
Activate the trauma team or Emergency Medicine for hemorrhage control, fracture stabilization, or operative management.
do_not: Do not move the patient unnecessarily.
Do not remove embedded objects.
Do not give food or drink.
stabilization_steps: Maintain cervical spine and full-body precautions until clearance is complete.
Continue hemodynamic monitoring, pain control, and serial examination for evolving injury.
Prepare for procedural hemorrhage control, fracture stabilization, or operative intervention under Emergency Medicine.
emergency_protocols.follow_up_care: Trauma or orthopedic follow-up for Road Traffic Trauma with wound care, repeat imaging, rehabilitation, and functional recovery planning.
emergency_protocols.remarks: For Road Traffic Trauma, do not remove embedded objects or over-manipulate fractures; delayed bleeding, compartment syndrome, or spinal injury can appear after the initial survey.

emergency_protocols.description: Thermal Burn usually develops after thermal, chemical, electrical, or inhalation exposure injures the skin and deeper tissues. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and burn depth/total body surface area while providing analgesia.
Consult Emergency Medicine or the burn team early for inhalation injury, large surface area burns, or electrical and chemical damage.
do_not: Do not apply ice or home remedies.
Do not pop blisters.
Do not delay airway review for inhalation injury.
stabilization_steps: Monitor airway edema, urine output, pain, and perfusion closely.
Use fluid resuscitation, wound coverage, and decontamination specific to the burn type.
Escalate to burn unit or ICU for inhalation injury, major surface area burns, or electrical damage.
emergency_protocols.follow_up_care: Burn service follow-up for Thermal Burn with dressings, scar prevention, graft review, rehabilitation, and infection surveillance.
emergency_protocols.remarks: For Thermal Burn, ice, ointments, and delayed airway reassessment can worsen outcomes; chemical or electrical exposure may continue to injure tissue after the visible burn.
